```{=html}
<!-- SECTION 0: START HERE -->
<section id="tab-start" class="tab-pane active" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="btn-tab-start">
  
  <div class="enso-section-header">
    <span class="enso-section-eyebrow">START HERE &bull; USER GUIDE &amp; PHYSICAL TELECONNECTIONS</span>
    <h2 class="enso-section-title">Section 0 &bull; How to Use the Kenya ENSO Explorer</h2>
    <p class="enso-section-intro">
      An empirical climate intelligence and decision-support system linking large-scale equatorial ocean dynamics (Pacific ENSO, Indian Ocean Dipole, and Western Pacific Gradient) to county-level agricultural production, rangeland forage resilience, flood inundation, and humanitarian emergency vulnerability across Kenya's 47 counties.
    </p>
  </div>

  <!-- Operational Disclaimer Banner -->
  <div class="enso-insight warning" style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;">
    <strong>Statutory Authority &amp; Forecast Boundary:</strong> The ENSO Explorer is an empirical research and risk assessment platform designed for climate rationale development, long-term contingency planning, and adaptation financing. It is <strong>NOT an operational daily weather forecast or statutory seasonal warning</strong>. For official, binding meteorological advisories and early warnings in Kenya, consult the statutory authority: the <strong>Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA; formerly KMD)</strong> under the <strong>Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026</strong> at <a href="https://meteo.go.ke" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="text-decoration: underline; font-weight: 600;">meteo.go.ke</a> and the <strong>IGAD Climate Prediction &amp; Applications Centre (ICPAC)</strong> at <a href="https://www.icpac.net" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="text-decoration: underline; font-weight: 600;">icpac.net</a>.
  </div>

  <!-- Executive County Brief & 2-Page Print/PDF Export (KE-48 / Decision D55) -->
  <div id="section-executive-brief" class="executive-brief-container" style="margin-bottom: 2rem;">
    <div id="sec0ExecutiveBriefHost">
      <div style="padding: 2.5rem 1.5rem; text-align: center; color: #64748b; font-size: 0.90rem;">
        <span class="spinner-border spinner-border-sm" role="status" aria-hidden="true" style="margin-right: 0.5rem;"></span>
        Loading Executive County Climate Brief &amp; 2-Page Anticipatory Action Matrix&hellip;
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- 3-Step Decision Path -->
  <div class="enso-figure-card">
    <div class="enso-figure-header">
      <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
        <h3 class="enso-figure-title" style="font-size: 1.15rem; color: #0f172a;">Three-Step Decision Workflow for County Officials &amp; Proposal Writers</h3>
        <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Follow this structured path to translate planetary climate signals into actionable county investment priorities and defensible adaptation finance rationales (GCF, AF, GEF, CIDP).</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="start-step-grid">
      <div class="start-step-card">
        <div class="step-header">
          <span class="step-badge">1</span>
          <h4 class="step-title">Select County &amp; Season</h4>
        </div>
        <p>Use the sticky control toolbar above to choose your target county and primary agricultural season (<strong>OND Short Rains</strong> or <strong>MAM Long Rains</strong>). Inspect Section 1 to review official KNBS crop and livestock baselines, modeled production value, and multi-dimensional vulnerability rankings.</p>
        <button type="button" class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="switchTab('tab-profile')" style="margin-top: 0.25rem;">Open County context &rarr;</button>
      </div>

      <div class="start-step-card">
        <div class="step-header">
          <span class="step-badge">2</span>
          <h4 class="step-title">Inspect Seasonal Outlook</h4>
        </div>
        <p>Check the live NOAA CPC equatorial ocean state probabilities and view the top historical analogue seasons ranked by Euclidean distance in joint ocean-temperature space. Examine empirical tercile shifts and multi-hazard outcomes from the most similar historical seasons.</p>
        <button type="button" class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="switchTab('tab-outlook')" style="margin-top: 0.25rem;">Open Seasonal outlook &rarr;</button>
      </div>

      <div class="start-step-card">
        <div class="step-header">
          <span class="step-badge">3</span>
          <h4 class="step-title">Review Historical Evidence</h4>
        </div>
        <p>Examine 44-year CHIRPS rainfall distributions, satellite raster history (NDVI, SAR flood, WRSI), and audited KNBS harvest shocks across past ocean states. Build empirical causal baselines that satisfy donor review standards without relying on ungrounded assumptions.</p>
        <button type="button" class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="switchTab('tab-graphs')" style="margin-top: 0.25rem;">Explore Climate evidence &rarr;</button>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- The Three Equatorial Drivers Explained in Plain Language -->
  <div class="enso-figure-card">
    <div class="enso-figure-header">
      <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
        <h3 class="enso-figure-title" style="font-size: 1.15rem; color: #0f172a;">Understanding Kenya's Planetary Teleconnections in Plain Language</h3>
        <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Kenya's bimodal rainfall is governed by three distinct ocean and atmospheric teleconnection engines operating across thousands of miles of tropical ocean.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="driver-card-grid">
      <div class="driver-card enso-card">
        <div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 0.4rem;">
          <h4 style="margin: 0; font-size: 0.95rem; font-weight: 700; color: #0369a1;">ENSO (Pacific Ocean)</h4>
          <span style="font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 700; background: #e0f2fe; color: #0284c7; padding: 1px 6px; border-radius: 4px;">RONI Index</span>
        </div>
        <p style="font-size: 0.84rem; color: #334155; margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0; line-height: 1.45;">
          <strong>El Niño–Southern Oscillation:</strong> The warming (<em>El Niño</em>) and cooling (<em>La Niña</em>) of surface waters across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific. In Kenya, El Niño shifts the atmospheric Walker circulation, strongly favoring above-normal rainfall during the <strong>OND Short Rains</strong> (flood risk), whereas La Niña strongly favors severe drought.
        </p>
        <div style="font-size: 0.74rem; color: #64748b; border-top: 1px solid #f1f5f9; padding-top: 0.35rem;">
          <em>Governing metric: Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI)</em>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="driver-card iod-card">
        <div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 0.4rem;">
          <h4 style="margin: 0; font-size: 0.95rem; font-weight: 700; color: #b45309;">IOD (Indian Ocean)</h4>
          <span style="font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 700; background: #fef3c7; color: #d97706; padding: 1px 6px; border-radius: 4px;">DMI Index</span>
        </div>
        <p style="font-size: 0.84rem; color: #334155; margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0; line-height: 1.45;">
          <strong>Indian Ocean Dipole:</strong> An east-west temperature see-saw across the equatorial Indian Ocean. A <strong>Positive IOD (+IOD)</strong> warms the western Indian Ocean near Kenya, pumping vast moisture inland. When a +IOD co-occurs with El Niño (as in 1997, 2006, and 2023)—or occurs as an extreme standalone event during ENSO-neutral conditions (as in 2019)—it causes historic mega-floods. Negative IOD (-IOD) exacerbates drought.
        </p>
        <div style="font-size: 0.74rem; color: #64748b; border-top: 1px solid #f1f5f9; padding-top: 0.35rem;">
          <em>Governing metric: Dipole Mode Index (DMI)</em>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="driver-card wnp-card">
        <div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 0.4rem;">
          <h4 style="margin: 0; font-size: 0.95rem; font-weight: 700; color: #047857;">Western-V (Western Pacific)</h4>
          <span style="font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 700; background: #d1fae5; color: #059669; padding: 1px 6px; border-radius: 4px;">WNP Metric</span>
        </div>
        <p style="font-size: 0.84rem; color: #334155; margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0; line-height: 1.45;">
          <strong>Western Pacific Gradient:</strong> A sea-surface temperature and convective gradient across the Western North Pacific that drives East Africa's <strong>MAM Long Rains</strong>. During MAM, canonical Pacific ENSO correlations decouple across Kenya, and the Western-V mode takes precedence in modulating monsoon onset and moisture transport.
        </p>
        <div style="font-size: 0.74rem; color: #64748b; border-top: 1px solid #f1f5f9; padding-top: 0.35rem;">
          <em>Governing metric: Western North Pacific anomaly (WNP)</em>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- Spatial & Seasonal Disclaimers -->
    <div style="background: #f8fafc; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.85rem 1rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
      <h5 style="margin: 0 0 0.35rem 0; font-size: 0.86rem; font-weight: 700; color: #0f172a;">Spatial &amp; Seasonal Regime Notice: Why "One Rule for Kenya" Fails</h5>
      <p style="margin: 0; font-size: 0.82rem; color: #475569; line-height: 1.5;">
        While El Niño brings surplus moisture to northern pastoral ASALs (Marsabit, Wajir, Garissa) and eastern lowlands during OND, western Kenya (Lake Victoria basin, Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu) follows a distinct rainfall regime with substantial June–August (JJA) rainfall governed by Congo moisture fluxes. Always examine county-specific climatology (Section 1) rather than applying national generalizations.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
```

```{=html}
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Table 1.1</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">
                Sub-County Administrative, Demographic &amp; Climatological Baseline — <span class="county-name-txt">Marsabit</span> (<span id="subcounty-count-txt">4</span> Constituencies)
              </h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">
              Official IEBC parliamentary constituencies (COD-AB adm2 boundaries), KNBS 2019 Census &amp; 2026 projections (distributed by WorldPop 100 m), and 30-year CHIRPS v3 (1991–2020) seasonal rainfall climatology.
            </p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Controls for Table 1.1 (View: Table | Plot, Variable selector) -->
        <div class="enso-control-bar" id="subControlsHost"></div>

        <!-- Dynamic Host for Table or Plot -->
        <div id="subcountyContentHost" style="min-height: 180px; margin-top: 0.5rem;"></div>

        <!-- Host for Table 1.1 Footer & CSV Download -->
        <div id="table11FooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Standard Details Fold for Table 1.1 -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('knbs_napr')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="fold-content-inner">
            <h5>Data Sources &amp; Administrative Framework</h5>
            <p>Geographic land area, population headcounts, and administrative ward boundaries are established under the <em>Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 Kenya Population &amp; Housing Census</em> (Volume I, Volume II &amp; Volume IV) and the <em>Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC)</em> official gazette.</p>
            <h5>Boundary Universes &amp; Sub-County Nomenclature</h5>
            <p><strong>IEBC Electoral Constituencies vs. KNBS Administrative Sub-Counties:</strong> The 290 sub-county units mapped across this atlas represent official <strong>IEBC parliamentary constituencies</strong> (standardized as UN OCHA COD-AB Level 2 boundaries). In national statistical reporting, KNBS designates 345 administrative sub-counties. In certain counties, these universes diverge: for instance, Marsabit comprises 4 electoral constituencies (Laisamis, Moyale, North Horr, and Saku) corresponding to 7 KNBS administrative sub-counties. Both spatial definitions are administratively recognized; however, because KNBS does not publish polygon geometries for the 345 administrative sub-counties, all high-resolution spatial overlays in this explorer utilize the authoritative 290 IEBC constituency boundaries.</p>
            <h5>Population Re-Levelling &amp; Spatial Disaggregation</h5>
            <ul>
              <li><strong>KNBS County Level Re-Levelling:</strong> Raw unconstrained WorldPop raster sums nationally total ~55.1 million, exceeding Kenya's 2019 census population (47.56 million). All population totals in this atlas are rigorously re-levelled to official KNBS county totals (2019 Census headcount and 2026 KNBS projections).</li>
              <li><strong>Within-County Spatial Distribution:</strong> Population headcounts are distributed across constituencies using WorldPop 100 m constrained residential building footprint shares. Within each county, constituency shares are anchored to the 2020 baseline distribution, while county growth rates track official KNBS demographic projections.</li>
              <li><strong>Dominant Season Derivation &amp; Equimodal Regimes:</strong> Seasonality classification is derived from the 30-year CHIRPS v3 (1991–2020) WMO climatological baseline. Sub-counties are classified into three distinct physical rainfall regimes:
                <ul>
                  <li><strong>Bimodal (Equimodal):</strong> Where MAM and OND seasonal accumulations differ by less than 25 mm or each season accounts for 45%–55% of the total bimodal volume (e.g. Saku in Marsabit: 289.7 mm MAM vs. 279.0 mm OND, 50.9% vs. 49.1%). In these balanced transition zones, neither season overwhelms the other, and pastoral forage replenishment depends critically on both rainfall windows.</li>
                  <li><strong>MAM (Long Rains):</strong> Where MAM accounts for &gt;55% of bimodal rainfall and exceeds OND by at least 25 mm (characteristic of western Kenya, central highlands, and Rift Valley).</li>
                  <li><strong>OND (Short Rains):</strong> Where OND accounts for &gt;55% of bimodal rainfall and exceeds MAM by at least 25 mm (characteristic of eastern pastoral lowlands including Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, and Tana River).</li>
                </ul>
              </li>
              <li><strong>Proposal &amp; Finance Alignment:</strong> County demographics and surface area figures align directly with the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA) Third Basis for Revenue Sharing formula and County Integrated Development Plans (CIDPs).</li>
            </ul>
          </div>
        </details>
      </div>

            <div class="fold-content-inner">
              <h5>Data Sources &amp; Ingestion Pipeline</h5>
              <p>Official county production statistics are extracted from the <em>Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) National Agricultural Produce Reports (NAPR 2019–2024 editions)</em>, Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) rice statistics, and the <em>2019 Kenya Population &amp; Housing Census Volume IV</em> (Distribution of Population by Socio-Economic Characteristics).</p>
              <h5>Audit Trail &amp; Reconciliation Protocol</h5>
              <ul>
                <li><strong>Dual-Engine Extraction:</strong> Official published report tables were extracted via dual PDF table engines (PyMuPDF and pdfplumber) with character-level coordinate verification and automated OCR cross-checks.</li>
                <li><strong>National Additivity Reconciliation:</strong> For every crop and livestock species, sub-national county values are audited against published national totals to ensure the sum of counties equals the published national figure within ±0.05% rounding tolerance.</li>
                <li><strong>Crucial Protocol: Blank &ne; Zero:</strong> An unsurveyed county or commodity in a specific reporting cycle is coded as missing (<code>NaN</code> / <code>∅</code> marker), NOT zero. A reported zero denotes an active survey recording zero yield. For arid rangeland counties (e.g., Marsabit, Turkana), rainfed crop farming is concentrated in isolated agro-pastoral sub-counties (e.g. Mount Marsabit / Saku); missing years reflect non-surveyed cycles rather than complete crop failure.</li>
                <li><strong>Administrative Statistics Baseline:</strong> These official statistics published by KNBS provide the recognized administrative baseline for county planning (CIDP) and project design documentation.</li>
              </ul>
            </div>
          </details>
        </div>

      <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-vop-card">
        <div class="enso-figure-header">
          <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 1.2</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">Spatially Modeled Value of Production Portfolio (IFPRI MapSPAM &amp; FAO GLW4) — <span class="county-name-txt">Marsabit</span></h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Gross agricultural capital portfolio in nominal 2021 USD (<code>vop_nominal-usd21</code>; undeflated) modeled via IFPRI MapSPAM (1 km crops) and FAO GLW4 (1 km livestock).</p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Controls for Figure 1.2 (View: Ranked commodities | Sub-county map, Sector filter) -->
        <div class="enso-control-bar" id="fig12ControlsHost"></div>

        <!-- Content Host for Figure 1.2 (Macro bar + Ranked Plot OR Sub-County Blocked State) -->
        <div id="fig12ContentHost" style="min-height: 240px; margin-top: 0.5rem;"></div>

        <div class="enso-insight warning" style="margin-top: 1rem;">
          <strong>Methodological Boundary &amp; Valuation Caveats:</strong> MapSPAM and GLW4 provide downscaled econometric distributions expressed on a <strong>Nominal 2021 USD</strong> basis (<code>vop_nominal-usd21</code>; undeflated). Because values are undeflated, cross-timeframe comparisons conflate macroeconomic price inflation with physical hazard shifts. While downscaled using global spatial priors, both layers are anchored to national agricultural census baselines (IFPRI MapSPAM 2020 v1r2 and FAO GLW4 2020, valued at 2019&ndash;23 national farm-gate prices: FAOSTAT&rsquo;s implied price with cited corrections, method in <code>hazards_prototype/docs/methods/nominal_price_method.md</code>), so national totals align with FAOSTAT (livestock reconciles at 1.00 since the September 2026 republication, <code>hazards_prototype#30</code>). <strong>Species Scope (Exclusion of Camels):</strong> FAO GLW4 maps cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, and poultry, but <em>excludes camels</em>. In camel-pastoral northern ASALs (Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa), modeled livestock capital represents ruminants and poultry only; total pastoral wealth is substantially higher when including camel herds (see Section 1.1 for official KNBS census numbers). These modeled totals remain essential for demonstrating to international donors that livestock represents 90%–97% of agricultural wealth in pastoral ASALs (directing adaptation finance proportionally to pastoral resilience while safeguarding vital highland agro-pastoral cropping sanctuaries like Saku and Moyale). However, because they are modeled from global priors, they <strong>must not be cited as subcounty administrative census statistics</strong>. Use Section 1.1 for legal administrative census numbers.
        </div>

        <!-- Host for Figure 1.2 Footer & Download -->
        <div id="fig12FooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Section 1.2 Folded Methodology & Provenance -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('exposure_vop')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="fold-content-inner">
            <h5>Data Sources &amp; Modeling Prior</h5>
            <p>Crop capital distributions are modeled from the <em>IFPRI Spatial Production Allocation Model (MapSPAM 2020 v1r2)</em> at 1 km resolution. Livestock capital distributions are downscaled from the <em>FAO Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW4)</em> at 1 km resolution, disaggregated across cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, and poultry. Note: FAO GLW4 does not model camels, an indispensable pastoral capital asset in northern ASALs (see Section 1.1 for official KNBS camel census counts).</p>
            <h5>Econometric Normalization &amp; Scope</h5>
            <ul>
              <li><strong>Nominal Currency Basis (<code>vop_nominal-usd21</code>):</strong> All production outputs and herd headcounts are monetized into <strong>Nominal 2021 USD</strong> (undeflated) at 2019&ndash;23 national farm-gate prices (crops: FAOSTAT&rsquo;s implied price with producer-price fallback and cited evidence pins; livestock: FAOSTAT producer prices). Because this series is undeflated, multi-year comparisons mix macroeconomic price inflation with climate hazard shifts.</li>
              <li><strong>Price Method Update (2026-10-06):</strong> The upstream exposure tables were republished with a revised nominal price method (<code>hazards_prototype#38&ndash;40</code>); the livestock reconciliation defect (<code>hazards_prototype#30</code>) was resolved in September 2026. The hazard-exposure layer was re-baked on the same prices the same day, so exposed-value shares are consistent with these totals (Kenya robusta coffee excepted: one Lake Victoria border cell is attributed to Uganda in the hazard layer).</li>
              <li><strong>Spatial Zonal Aggregation:</strong> 1 km grid cells are zonal-summed over official Kenya county boundary vectors to establish gross agricultural capital endowments.</li>
              <li><strong>Spatial Nuance:</strong> In arid rangelands (e.g., Marsabit, Turkana, Wajir, Mandera), rainfed field cropping is not uniformly spread; it is clustered in highland agro-pastoral pockets (e.g. Saku and Moyale in Marsabit) or irrigated river corridors.</li>
              <li><strong>Strategic Financing Role:</strong> In pastoral ASAL counties, pastoralist herds represent 90%–97% of agricultural Value of Production (VoP). This establishes the macroeconomic evidence required by GCF and Adaptation Fund investment boards to prioritize rangeland water retention, index-based livestock insurance (IBLI), and veterinary cold chains over unviable crop irrigation schemes.</li>
            </ul>
          </div>
        </details>
```

```{=html}
              Table 2.1 &bull; Two-Season Compound Historical Outcome Record (MAM + OND)

          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('driver_indices')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">
            <div class="decision-box">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why Analogue Multi-Hazard Diagnostics?</span>
                <span class="rationale-tag">Empirical Grounding</span>
              </div>
              <p class="rationale-text">
                Single-variable rainfall forecasts fail to capture compound hazard transmission. By coupling historical ocean states with satellite-derived pasture vegetative flushes (MODIS NDVI) and pastoral grain exchange rates (FEWS NET/NDMA Terms of Trade), county directors can evaluate how previous analogous seasons impacted food security, livestock markets, and emergency response budgets.
              </p>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid">
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Standardized Predictor Space:</strong> Nearest neighbours are ranked using normalized Euclidean distance in joint RONI + DMI space.</li>
                  <li><strong>Two-Season Memory:</strong> Pasture and livestock conditions depend heavily on whether the preceding MAM Long Rains were wet or dry.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Market Context:</strong> Terms of trade reflect historical commodity price regimes and macro inflation that may differ from current economic baselines.</li>
                  <li><strong>Local Variations:</strong> Micro-climates and intra-seasonal dry spells can modulate local outcomes even in wet analogue years.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="fold-footer-bar">
              <div><strong>Primary Source:</strong> NOAA CPC ERSSTv6 &bull; CHIRPS v3 &bull; MODIS NDVI &bull; NDMA / FEWS NET</div>
              <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('driver_indices')">Driver Indices Spec &rarr;</button>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </details>

        <p class="statutory-notice-body">
          Pursuant to the <strong>Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026</strong> (assented March 13, 2026), the <strong>Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA; official products may retain Kenya Meteorological Department/KMD branding during transition)</strong> is the statutory designated authority legally mandated to formulate, issue, and regulate all official weather forecasts, seasonal climate outlooks, and operational early warning advisories in the Republic of Kenya.
        </p>
        <div class="statutory-boundary-note">
          <strong>Mandate Boundary &amp; Platform Role:</strong> The Adaptation Atlas does not produce independent operational forecasts or issue unilateral disaster directives. It provides historical analogue scenarios and teleconnection risk diagnostics. <strong>County governments, disaster committees, and development partners must strictly anchor all operational triggers and contingency funding to official KMSA bulletins and localized advisories from County Directors of Meteorology (CDMs).</strong>
```

```{=html}
<section id="tab-graphs" class="tab-pane" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="btn-tab-graphs">
      
      <!-- Section 3: Historical Climate Evidence (Part 3.1: Climate Graphs) -->
      <div class="enso-section-header" style="margin-bottom: 1.25rem;">
        <div class="enso-section-eyebrow">3 Historical Climate Evidence &bull; 3.1 Climate Graphs</div>
        <h2 class="enso-section-title">
          Section 3.1 &bull; Climate Graphs &amp; Empirical Contingency Distributions — <span class="county-name-txt">Marsabit</span>
        </h2>
        <p class="enso-section-lead">
          Multi-decadal seasonal precipitation climatology, SPEI-3 drought anomalies, and ocean driver contingency distributions.
        </p>
      </div>

      <!-- Plain-Language Explainer & Reading Guide Card -->
      <div class="card" style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem; background: #f8fafc; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius: 8px; padding: 1.15rem 1.35rem;">
        <div style="font-weight: 700; font-size: 0.92rem; color: #0f172a; margin-bottom: 0.45rem; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;">
          <span style="font-size: 1.1rem;">🧭</span>
          <span>How to Navigate Historical Climate Evidence &amp; Teleconnection Strength</span>
        </div>
        <p style="font-size: 0.84rem; color: #334155; line-height: 1.55; margin-bottom: 0.75rem;">
          Section 3 provides the empirical bedrock for county climate risk planning. Rather than relying solely on global climate model forecasts, this section catalogs what has actually happened across 44 years of satellite and ocean observations (1981–2024).
        </p>
        <div style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(260px, 1fr)); gap: 0.85rem; font-size: 0.8rem; line-height: 1.5;">
          <div style="background: #ffffff; padding: 0.75rem 0.9rem; border-radius: 6px; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;">
            <strong style="color: #0369a1;">1. Questions Answered:</strong>
            <ul style="margin: 0.3rem 0 0; padding-left: 1.1rem; color: #475569;">
              <li>How dependable is the ENSO / IOD teleconnection in this specific county?</li>
              <li>What are the empirical odds of a Wetter vs. Drier season during an El Niño or +IOD?</li>
              <li>Which sub-counties face severe 100-year riverine flood exposure?</li>
            </ul>
          </div>
          <div style="background: #ffffff; padding: 0.75rem 0.9rem; border-radius: 6px; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;">
            <strong style="color: #0369a1;">2. Reading Sequence:</strong>
            <ol style="margin: 0.3rem 0 0; padding-left: 1.1rem; color: #475569;">
              <li><strong>Fig 3.1:</strong> Multi-decadal rainfall &amp; SPEI-3 anomaly history.</li>
              <li><strong>Fig 3.2:</strong> Empirical contingency probabilities (tercile odds).</li>
              <li><strong>Fig 3.3:</strong> Candidate driver regression &amp; correlation ranking.</li>
              <li><strong>Fig 3.4 &amp; 3.5:</strong> High-resolution spatial raster grids &amp; flood exposure.</li>
            </ol>
          </div>
          <div style="background: #ffffff; padding: 0.75rem 0.9rem; border-radius: 6px; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;">
            <strong style="color: #0369a1;">3. Physical Limits &amp; Caveats:</strong>
            <ul style="margin: 0.3rem 0 0; padding-left: 1.1rem; color: #475569;">
              <li>Non-stationarity: Past frequencies may shift under greenhouse warming.</li>
              <li>Orographic satellite underestimation around isolated mountain massifs.</li>
              <li>SAR blindspots: Sentinel-1 orbital passes miss brief flash flood events.</li>
            </ul>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>

      <!-- Geography Mode Toolbar Host -->
      <div id="sec3GeoModeHost" style="margin-bottom: 1rem;"></div>

      <!-- Sub-County Comparison Panel Host -->
      <div id="sec3SubcountyCompareHost" style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;"></div>

      <!-- Section 3.1: Multi-Decadal Precipitation & SPEI Climatology -->
      <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-rain-climatology">
        <div class="enso-figure-header">
          <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 3.1</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">Multi-Decadal Precipitation Climatology &amp; Standardized Anomalies (CHIRPS v3 &amp; SPEI-3)</h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Historical seasonal rainfall and SPEI-3 anomaly time series (1981–2024) with ocean teleconnection markers.</p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Toolbar Host for Figure 3.1 Controls -->
        <div id="sec21ControlsHost" class="enso-control-bar"></div>

        <!-- Live Empirical Ocean Phase Chips Host (fallback host) -->
        <div id="sec21PhaseChipsHost"></div>

        <!-- Host Div for Figure 3.1 Reactive Plot -->
        <div id="plotRainHost" style="min-height: 380px; width: 100%;"></div>

        <!-- Figure 3.1 plotFooter Host -->
        <div id="fig31FooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Expandable Folded Methods & Assumptions -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('chirps_seasonal')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">
            <div class="decision-box">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                <span class="rationale-tag">Spatial Continuity Rationale</span>
              </div>
              <p class="rationale-text">
                <strong>The "Best Available Data" Reality:</strong> Ground-based meteorological stations in northern Kenya are extremely sparse—often fewer than one active, reliable rain gauge per 20,000 km². Relying purely on physical weather stations creates massive blind spots across ASAL pastoral rangelands. CHIRPS v3 (UCSB/CHC) blends cold-cloud duration satellite infrared with reporting stations to create continuous 5 km grids spanning 1981 to present. Satellite-gauge blending is the physically grounded standard to track pixel-level subcounty drought and flood anomalies continuously across Kenya.
              </p>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid">
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>WMO Climatological Baseline:</strong> Anomalies are computed against the 1991–2020 normal period (30 years) to conform to WMO standard reference rules.</li>
                  <li><strong>Linear Detrending:</strong> Long-term greenhouse gas warming trends are detrended before calculating ENSO/IOD teleconnection correlations to isolate interannual ocean forcing.</li>
                  <li><strong>Fixed Accumulation Windows:</strong> OND (Oct 1 – Dec 31) and MAM (Mar 1 – May 31) are treated as rigid seasonal boundaries matching agricultural calendars.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Orographic Underestimation:</strong> Thermal infrared satellite estimates systematically underestimate localized orographic rainfall around isolated mountain massifs (e.g. Mt. Marsabit, Mt. Kulal).</li>
                  <li><strong>SPEI Evapotranspiration:</strong> SPEI-3 utilizes Hargreaves-Samani PET, which can over-estimate evaporative demand during hyper-thermal arid spells.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="fold-footer-bar">
              <div><strong>Primary Source:</strong> CHIRPS v3 (0.05°) &bull; Vicente-Serrano SPEI-3 &bull; <code>s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=precipitation/source=chirps-v3/</code></div>
              <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('chirps_seasonal')">CHIRPS Spec &rarr;</button>
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('spei_seasonal')">SPEI-3 Spec &rarr;</button>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </details>
      </div>

      <!-- Section 3.1B: Consecutive Seasonal Rainfall Sequences & Compounding Drought Runs -->
      <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-consecutive-sequence" style="margin-top: 1.5rem;">
        <div class="enso-figure-header">
          <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 3.1B</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">Consecutive Seasonal Rainfall Sequences &amp; Compounding Drought Runs (1982–2025)</h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Sequential evaluation of compound multi-season drought risk across consecutive production years (OND(Y−1) &rarr; MAM(Y)) and unbroken runs of sub-normal rainfall.</p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Plain-Language How to Read -->
        <div class="enso-insight info" style="margin-bottom: 0.85rem; font-size: 0.84rem;">
          <strong>How to Read the Sequence View:</strong> Production year Y pairs the preceding Short Rains (OND of year Y−1) with the following Long Rains (MAM of year Y), matching the KNBS production-year convention where both harvests land within year Y. Each season is standardized independently against its own 1991–2020 WMO climatological baseline (never pooled). Cells are colored by standardized anomaly (z): <em>Dry</em> (z &lt; &minus;0.5, red), <em>Normal</em> (&minus;0.5 &le; z &le; +0.5, gray), and <em>Wet</em> (z &gt; +0.5, blue). <strong>Double failure years (dry / dry)</strong> are flagged distinctly as compounding multi-season drought emergencies. The run-length bar tracks unbroken consecutive seasons of sub-normal rainfall.
        </div>

        <!-- Toolbar Host for Figure 3.1B Controls -->
        <div id="sec31bControlsHost" class="enso-control-bar"></div>

        <!-- KPI / Summary Highlights Host -->
        <div id="sec31bKpiHost" style="margin-top: 0.65rem; margin-bottom: 0.85rem;"></div>

        <!-- Host Div for Figure 3.1B Reactive Plot / Domino Strip -->
        <div id="plotSequenceHost" style="min-height: 440px; width: 100%;"></div>

        <!-- Figure 3.1B plotFooter Host -->
        <div id="fig31bFooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Expandable Folded Methods & Assumptions -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('chirps_seasonal')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">
            <div class="decision-box">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                <span class="rationale-tag">Sequential Compounding Rationale</span>
              </div>
              <p class="rationale-text">
                <strong>Sequences Matter More Than Averages:</strong> In East African bimodal climate regimes, single-season climate shocks can often be absorbed by household food reserves, pastoral herd condition, or regional grain trade. However, consecutive failures across both seasons trigger systemic collapse: rangeland forage deficits compound, livestock mortality accelerates, and rainfed staple harvests fail back-to-back. Averaging seasonal totals (such as OND+MAM) obscures this physical reality—a wet season and a catastrophic drought average out to "near-normal," hiding critical humanitarian risk. Evaluating the chronological sequence OND(Y−1) &rarr; MAM(Y) preserves the true multi-season shock trajectory.
              </p>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid">
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>KNBS Production Year Pairing:</strong> Year Y pairs the preceding Short Rains OND(Y−1) with Long Rains MAM(Y). Both harvests occur within calendar year Y, matching national agricultural accounting (KNBS NAPR) and HarvestStat Africa planted-year conventions.</li>
                  <li><strong>Independent Seasonal Moments:</strong> OND and MAM are standardized separately against their own 1991–2020 normal period (WMO standard). The distributions have different means and variances and are never pooled.</li>
                  <li><strong>Categorical Thresholds:</strong> Consistent with standard meteorological tercile definitions: Dry (z &lt; &minus;0.5), Wet (z &gt; +0.5), and Near-normal (&minus;0.5 &le; z &le; +0.5).</li>
                  <li><strong>Unbroken Pastoral Stress Runs:</strong> Cumulative run length walks seasons in true chronological order (&hellip;OND(Y−1), MAM(Y), OND(Y), MAM(Y+1)&hellip;) counting unbroken consecutive sub-normal seasons (z &lt; &minus;0.5). Forage depletion compounds across seasons and does not reset at the calendar year.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Calendar Variations in 4 Counties:</strong> The production-year pairing convention (OND(Y−1) + MAM(Y)) is standard across 43 counties but knowingly differs in 4 counties where the cropping calendar is unimodal or has alternate planting regimes (<code>project_season_year_convention</code>).</li>
                  <li><strong>Microclimatic Aggregation:</strong> County-level spatial averages blend agro-ecological zones; localized pastoral rangelands may experience multi-season drought even when high-elevation agricultural belts register near-normal rainfall.</li>
                  <li><strong>Gaps vs. Zeros:</strong> Missing seasons are preserved as explicit gaps and never imputed as zero rainfall or normal conditions.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="fold-footer-bar">
              <div><strong>Primary Source:</strong> CHIRPS v3 (0.05°) &bull; HarvestStat Africa &bull; KNBS NAPR &bull; <code>s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=precipitation/source=chirps-v3/</code></div>
              <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('chirps_seasonal')">CHIRPS Spec &rarr;</button>
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('harveststat_crop')">HarvestStat Spec &rarr;</button>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </details>
      </div>

      <!-- Section 3.2: Empirical Contingency Matrix -->
      <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-tercile-contingency" style="margin-top: 1.5rem;">
        <div class="enso-figure-header">
          <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 3.2</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">Empirical Contingency Probability Matrix (Tercile Likelihood given Ocean Driver Strength)</h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Observed conditional probabilities of Wetter, Near-normal, or Drier seasons conditioned on ENSO, IOD, and Western-V intensity classes (1981–2024 record).</p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Plain-Language How to Read -->
        <div class="enso-insight info" style="margin-bottom: 0.85rem; font-size: 0.84rem;">
          <strong>How to Read Tercile Probabilities:</strong> Historical seasons are stratified into equal thirds based on 1991–2020 climatology: <em>Wetter</em> (top 33.3%), <em>Near-normal</em> (middle 33.3%), and <em>Drier</em> (bottom 33.3%). Under random chance or neutral ocean conditions, each tercile has an unconditional base rate of ~33%. Shifts away from 33% quantify the empirical teleconnection strength.
        </div>

        <!-- Toolbar Host for Figure 3.2 Controls -->
        <div id="sec22ControlsHost" class="enso-control-bar"></div>

        <!-- Host Div for Figure 3.2 Plot -->
        <div id="plotContingencyHost" style="min-height: 360px; width: 100%;"></div>

        <!-- Teleconnection Insight Box -->
        <div id="sec22InsightHost" style="margin-top: 0.75rem;"></div>

        <!-- Figure 3.2 plotFooter Host -->
        <div id="fig32FooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Expandable Folded Methods & Assumptions -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('teleconnections')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">
            <div class="decision-box">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                <span class="rationale-tag">Non-Parametric Teleconnection Evidence</span>
              </div>
              <p class="rationale-text">
                <strong>Honest Physical Limits:</strong> Standard linear correlation models oversimplify East African climate teleconnections because rainfall responses are asymmetric and non-linear. The empirical contingency matrix stratifies the historical 44-year record into discrete ocean driver intensity bands (Strong, Moderate, Neutral/Weak) and computes the exact empirical tercile distribution (Wetter / Near-normal / Drier) for each state. This gives planners non-parametric, physically transparent probabilities directly matching KMD 3-tier seasonal forecasts.
              </p>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid">
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Tercile Climatological Equal-Likelihood:</strong> Under climatology, each tercile (Wet, Near, Dry) has an unconditional base rate of 33.3% over the 1991–2020 normal period.</li>
                  <li><strong>Small-Sample Transparency:</strong> Groups with fewer than 4 historical seasons are explicitly flagged with an asterisk (*) to warn against interpreting isolated anecdotes as statistical proof.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Sample Size Constraints:</strong> Super El Niño and Super +IOD events are rare extremes (n = 3–5 events in 44 years), limiting sample sizes for extreme composite bins.</li>
                  <li><strong>MAM Driver Independence:</strong> The Western-V gradient partially decouples from equatorial Pacific ENSO during the Long Rains (MAM), reflecting subtropical Western North Pacific wave trains.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="fold-footer-bar">
              <div><strong>Primary Source:</strong> NOAA CPC ONI &bull; HadISST / ERSST DMI &bull; CHIRPS v3 Terciles &bull; <code>s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=indices/</code></div>
              <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('teleconnections')">Teleconnection Spec &rarr;</button>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </details>
      </div>

      <!-- Section 3.3: Oceanic Driver Teleconnection Relationships -->
      <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-driver-scatter" style="margin-top: 1.5rem;">
        <div class="enso-figure-header">
          <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 3.3</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">How Strongly Do Equatorial Ocean Temperatures Govern County Rainfall?</h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Candidate ocean driver comparison table, continuous bivariate scatter distribution, and linear regression across all 44 historical seasons (1981–2024).</p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Candidate Driver Comparison Table Host -->
        <div id="sec23DriverTableHost" style="margin-bottom: 1rem;"></div>

        <!-- Toolbar Host for Figure 3.3 Controls -->
        <div id="sec23ScatterControlsHost" class="enso-control-bar"></div>

        <!-- Stats Callout Host for Figure 3.3 -->
        <div id="sec23ScatterStatsHost" style="margin-top: 0.5rem;"></div>

        <!-- Host Div for Figure 3.3 Reactive Plot -->
        <div id="plotDriverScatterHost" style="min-height: 380px; width: 100%; margin-top: 0.5rem;"></div>

        <!-- Figure 3.3 plotFooter Host -->
        <div id="fig33FooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Expandable Folded Methods & Assumptions -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('teleconnections')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">
            <div class="decision-box">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                <span class="rationale-tag">Continuous Teleconnection Sensitivity</span>
              </div>
              <p class="rationale-text">
                <strong>Bridging Discrete Bins to Continuous Sensitivity:</strong> While contingency matrices (Figure 3.2) group ocean drivers into coarse categorical bins, climate finance proposal writers and disaster contingency planners require exact marginal response metrics: for every +0.5°C or +1.0°C rise in equatorial Pacific SST (RONI) or Western Indian Ocean SST (DMI), how many additional millimetres or percentage points of rainfall are expected? This continuous scatter plot and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression line across all 44 historical years (1981–2024) provides the empirical slope, Pearson correlation coefficient (r), coefficient of determination (R²), and two-tailed p-value.
              </p>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid">
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Climatological Normal:</strong> Anomalies are computed against the WMO standard 1991–2020 reference period.</li>
                  <li><strong>Linear Bivariate Modeling:</strong> OLS regression provides the linear teleconnection slope. Non-linear saturation effects during super-events (e.g. 1997, 2023) are visible as residual scatters from the trendline.</li>
                  <li><strong>Seasonal Alignment:</strong> OND rainfall is paired with OND ocean indices; MAM rainfall is paired with MAM ocean indices (Western-V / WNP).</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Statistical Power</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Collinearity:</strong> ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole often co-occur during OND (e.g. positive IOD + El Niño in 1997, 2006, and 2023, or standalone extreme +IOD during neutral ENSO in 2019). Raw bivariate r reflects combined ocean basin influence; check the candidate table for multi-driver variance.</li>
                  <li><strong>Outlier Leverage:</strong> Extreme years like 1997 and 2023 exert leverage on the slope; points are explicitly labeled to inspect leverage.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="fold-footer-bar">
              <div><strong>Primary Sources:</strong> NOAA CPC ONI &bull; HadISST DMI &bull; CHIRPS v3 &bull; <code>data/KE-enso-explorer/chirps_county.parquet</code></div>
              <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('teleconnections')">Teleconnection Spec &rarr;</button>
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('chirps_seasonal')">CHIRPS Spec &rarr;</button>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </details>
      </div>
</section>
```

```{=html}
              </div>
              <ul class="rationale-list" style="margin-top: 0.35rem;">
                <li><strong>Per-Year Facet Canvas:</strong> Renders 40+ years of high-resolution gridded satellite observations in an interactive multi-column grid, clipped to official IEBC county boundaries.</li>
                <li><strong>Ocean Teleconnection Tint:</strong> Each year card is subtly tinted by the standardized anomaly (<em>z</em>-score) of the selected oceanic driver (PRGn diverging palette by default: green for wet teleconnection states, purple for suppressing dry states).</li>
                <li><strong>Anomaly vs. Climatology:</strong> Rainfall displays standardized departure from the WMO 1991–2020 reference normal by default (&plusmn;300 mm scale), isolating true teleconnection impacts from baseline aridity.</li>
                <li><strong>Multi-Sensor Diagnostics:</strong> Switch between 5 earth observation systems to evaluate whether atmospheric moisture translated into surface drought (SPEI-3), vegetation biomass (NDVI), inundation (GFM), or crop satisfaction (WRSI).</li>
              </ul>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid" style="margin-top: 0.75rem;">
              <!-- Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats -->
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Module B: Assumptions, Limitations &amp; Caveats</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Reference Climatology Baseline:</strong> Rainfall anomalies are computed against 1991–2020 WMO standard normal. SPEI-3 is already standard-normalized; MODIS NDVI and Copernicus GFM do not have 30-year baselines.</li>
                  <li><strong>Copernicus GFM Record Length &amp; SAR Masking:</strong> Sentinel-1 SAR flood coverage spans only 2018–2025. It reflects recent flood-proneness and orbital pass timing, NOT long-term return-period magnitude. Value 255 (unobserved swath) is strictly excluded as NoData, never counted as dry.</li>
                  <li><strong>HTTP Range COG Streaming:</strong> GeoTIFF rasters are window-read on the fly via HTTP range requests against AWS S3 CloudFront, fetching only the county bounding box to preserve client memory.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>

              <!-- Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary -->
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Module C: Methods &amp; Analysis Summary</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Driver Independence (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell):</strong> Correlation chips display bivariate Pearson <em>r</em> alongside partial correlation (controlling for other drivers) to eliminate double-counting of collinear ENSO and IOD signals.</li>
                  <li><strong>Multi-Driver Linear Combination:</strong> Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression calculates the optimal multi-driver variance explained (adjusted <em>R</em>&sup2;), identifying whether joint monitoring beats single indices.</li>
                  <li><strong>Phase Intensity Gating:</strong> Categorical intensity presets filter analogue historical seasons at |<em>z</em>| &ge; 1.0&sigma; (moderate) and |<em>z</em>| &ge; 1.5&sigma; (strong/extreme) thresholds.</li>

The European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC) Global River Flood Hazard Maps v2.1 dataset provides 90 m hydrodynamic flood inundation modeling (2D LISFLOOD-FP forced by GloFAS v4 runoff, evaluating 10- to 500-year return periods; Baugh et al. 2024).           </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">

            <!-- Module A: Visual Interpretation & Capabilities -->
            <div class="doc-module-card">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Module A: Plot Capabilities &amp; Visual Interpretation</span>
              </div>
              <ul class="rationale-list" style="margin-top: 0.35rem;">
                <li><strong>Dual-Source Diagnostics:</strong> Toggle between observed satellite radar footprints (Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR curated across 2018–2025) and modelled probabilistic benchmarks (EC JRC Global River Flood Hazard Maps v2.1 10- to 500-year return periods).</li>
                <li><strong>Multi-Scenario Comparison:</strong> Select multiple return period checkboxes (10 to 500 years) to compare the non-linear expansion of inundated territory against built infrastructure.</li>
                <li><strong>Population Denominators:</strong> Headcounts reflect official KNBS census levels (2019 Census &amp; 2026 projections), distributed across constituencies using WorldPop 100 m residential building footprints.</li>
              </ul>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid" style="margin-top: 0.75rem;">
              <!-- Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats -->
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Module B: Assumptions, Limitations &amp; Caveats</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>HOT-OSM Volunteer Gaps:</strong> Health center and school locations originate from crowdsourced Humanitarian OpenStreetMap (HOT-OSM). In remote pastoral counties, crowdsourced coverage is incomplete. <strong>A value of zero exposed schools reflects absence of volunteer mapped points, NOT immunity to floods.</strong></li>
                  <li><strong>Geomorphic Drainage &amp; Flash Floods:</strong> GloFAS models riverine overtopping along major river channel networks (e.g., Tana, Athi, Nyando, Ewaso Ng'iro, Daua). However, in arid and semi-arid (ASAL) counties such as Marsabit, drainage is dominated by ephemeral sand-rivers (<em>laggas / wadis</em>) terminating into endorheic basins (Lake Turkana and the Chalbi Desert pan) rather than perennial river networks. Sudden convective cloudbursts flushing through these laggas are not fully captured by continental riverine models. Permanent waterbodies (Lake Turkana) and seasonal salt pans (Chalbi Desert) are masked out (HydroLAKES &amp; RCMRD land cover) to prevent conflating natural water surfaces with flooded assets.</li>
                  <li><strong>Stationarity Assumption:</strong> Return periods assume stationary hydrologic extremes over the 1979–2022 reanalysis window; intensifying warming may shift 100-year events into 50-year frequencies.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>

              <!-- Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary -->
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Module C: Methods &amp; Analysis Summary</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Hydrodynamic Routing:</strong> 2D LISFLOOD-FP hydrodynamic modeling (EC JRC Global River Flood Hazard Maps v2.1, 90 m, forced by GloFAS v4 runoff; Baugh et al. 2024), routing peak discharge across digital elevation models to compute flood water depth rasters for 10- to 500-year return periods.</li>
                  <li><strong>Spatial Exposure Intersect:</strong> Performed via DuckDB spatial polygon-in-raster operations, clipping depth surfaces at &ge; 0.15 m threshold across subcounty boundaries.</li>
                  <li><strong>Seasonal Flood Dynamics:</strong> Both OND and MAM produce severe riverine and flash flooding across Kenya. While OND flooding is strongly modulated by El Niño and positive IOD basin-wide surges, MAM seasons also generate catastrophic riverine flooding across the Tana, Nyando, and Athi basins (as demonstrated in MAM 2018 and MAM 2024, alongside pluvial flash floods and infrastructure failures).</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

              </div>
            </div>

          </div>
        </details>
```

```{=html}
        </h2>
        <p class="enso-section-subtitle">
          Quantifying how Pacific and Indian Ocean warming signals propagate through subnational crop yields, pastoral herd demography, market terms of trade, and hydrodynamic flood exposure.
        </p>
      </div>

          <div class="enso-figure-header">
            <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
              <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
                <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 4.1</span>
                <h3 class="enso-figure-title">Dual-Season Ocean Drivers vs. Agricultural &amp; Livestock Output — <span class="county-name-txt">Marsabit</span></h3>
              </div>
              <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Linking the bimodal climate signal (MAM Long Rains + OND Short Rains) to KNBS county agricultural production statistics and livestock outputs (2016–2024).</p>
            </div>
            <button class="provenance-link-btn" onclick="openMethodDrawer('knbs_napr')">Data &amp; Methodology</button>
          </div>

          <div class="enso-insight info" style="margin-bottom: 1.25rem;">
            <strong>The Bimodal Agricultural Attribution Reality:</strong> In Kenya's bimodal climate, annual crop production reported by KNBS is the composite result of two distinct seasonal harvests: the <strong>MAM Long Rains</strong> (planted Mar, harvested Jul/Aug, steered by the Western-V) and the <strong>OND Short Rains</strong> (planted Oct, harvested Jan/Feb of the following year, steered by IOD and ENSO). Single-season climate shocks can often be absorbed, but consecutive failures across both seasons trigger systemic collapse.
          </div>

          <!-- Figure 4.1 Controls & View Toggle Host -->
          <div id="sec31ViewControlsHost" style="margin-bottom: 0.85rem;"></div>

          <!-- Folded Methodology -->
          <details class="enso-more-details" style="margin-top: 1rem;">
            <summary>
              <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
              <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('knbs_napr')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
            </summary>
            <div class="methods-fold-content">
              <div class="decision-box">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                  <span class="rationale-tag">Official Subnational Series</span>
                </div>
                <p class="rationale-text">
                  <strong>The "Best Available Data" Reality:</strong> Subnational agricultural statistics in Kenya have historically been fragmented. We combine the official KNBS National Agricultural Production Reports (2019–2024) with HarvestStat Africa v1.2 (1965–2024, Lee et al. 2025, Nature Scientific Data) to construct the first continuous, audited multi-decadal production series linked directly to ocean driver indices.
                </p>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-grid">
                <div class="rationale-col">
                  <div class="rationale-heading">
                    <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                  </div>
                  <ul class="rationale-list">
                    <li><strong>5-Year Rolling Climatological Baseline:</strong> Harvest anomalies are calculated relative to the preceding 5-year rolling median to account for gradual expansion in cultivated acreage.</li>
                    <li><strong>Lagged Harvest Accounting:</strong> OND Short Rains crops are planted in October and harvested in January/February of year t+1; this physical lag is explicitly harmonized in the annual statistics.</li>
                  </ul>
                </div>
                <div class="rationale-col">
                  <div class="rationale-heading">
                    <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                  </div>
                  <ul class="rationale-list">
                    <li><strong>ASAL Arid Zone Bias:</strong> In Marsabit, rainfed maize is cultivated almost exclusively on high-elevation microclimates (Mt. Marsabit and Moyale bluffs). Rangeland livestock output represents 95% of agricultural asset value.</li>
                    <li><strong>Cross-Edition Discrepancies:</strong> KNBS 2023-24 vs 2024-25 editions exhibit slight rebasings (median ratio 0.96); numbers are locked to latest published KNBS revisions.</li>
                  </ul>
                </div>
              </div>
              <div class="fold-footer-bar">
                <div><strong>Primary Sources:</strong> KNBS NAPR (2019–2024) &bull; HarvestStat Africa v1.2 &bull; CHIRPS v3 &bull; MODIS MOD13Q1</div>
                <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                  <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('knbs_napr')">KNBS NAPR Spec &rarr;</button>
                  <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('harveststat_crop')">HarvestStat Spec &rarr;</button>
                </div>
              </div>
            </div>
          </details>
        </div>

              </div>
              <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Evaluating observed range intervals, sample sizes, and average agricultural outputs conditioned on categorical ocean teleconnection states (KNBS audited survey years).</p>
            </div>
            <button class="provenance-link-btn" onclick="openMethodDrawer('knbs_napr')">Data &amp; Methodology</button>
          </div>

          <div style="background: #f8fafc; border-left: 3px solid #0284c7; padding: 0.85rem 1.15rem; border-radius: 0 4px 4px 0; margin-bottom: 1.25rem; font-size: 0.85rem; line-height: 1.6; color: #1e293b;">
            <strong>National Harvest-Aligned Attribution Convention:</strong> Production years are aligned to the seasons harvested within them: <strong>OND of the previous year (t−1) plus MAM of the reporting year (t)</strong>. KNBS does not publish its own convention; this alignment was selected by testing county maize yields against candidate season mappings (2019–2024). Short-rains drivers (ENSO, IOD) evaluate the state at OND(t−1); Long-rains drivers (Western-V) evaluate at MAM(t).<br/>
            <span style="font-size: 0.8rem; color: #64748b;"><em>Note on Eastern Counties:</em> In short-rains dominant counties (Tana River, Meru, Kitui, Makueni), OND of the reporting year (t) is the primary driver (r = 0.40) while MAM is negligible.</span>
          </div>

            <strong>Structural Season-Year Anchoring &amp; The Reporting Hole:</strong> In HarvestStat, every harvest is anchored to its <strong>planting year</strong>. Short Rains crops planted in October of year <em>t</em> and harvested in February/March of year <em>t+1</em> belong to year <em>t</em> &mdash; aligning them directly with OND rains and El Ni&ntilde;o / +IOD drivers. By default, the recent county era (<strong>2015–2024</strong>) is displayed; the full record includes a national statistical reporting gap (2002–2014) where subnational seasonal reporting lapsed.

                  <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                  <span class="rationale-tag">Harmonized Historical Records</span>
                </div>
                <p class="rationale-text">
                  <strong>The Longest Subnational Harvest Record:</strong> HarvestStat Africa v1.2 (Lee et al. 2025, <em>Nature Scientific Data</em>) digitizes and harmonizes subnational Ministry of Agriculture archives back to 1990. Splitting data into Long and Short Rains allows direct testing of whether wet or dry planting seasons translated into above- or below-normal harvest outcomes over three decades.
                </p>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-grid">
                <div class="rationale-col">
                  <div class="rationale-heading">
                    <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                  </div>
                  <ul class="rationale-list">
                    <li><strong>Era-Median Baseline (% of a Usual Year):</strong> Anomalies are computed relative to the median of each distinct administrative era (&ge;7 clean seasons required): 1990–2001 (district-era records remapped to 47 counties) or 2015–2024 (county records).</li>
                    <li><strong>Quality Control Flagging:</strong> Upstream QC-flagged observations (flag &gt; 0) are shown with dashed red outlines and excluded from medians and summary statistics.</li>
                  </ul>
                </div>
                <div class="rationale-col">
                  <div class="rationale-heading">
                    <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                  </div>
                  <ul class="rationale-list">
                    <li><strong>The 2002–2014 Statistical Gap:</strong> Between 2002 and 2014, subnational seasonal crop monitoring was not systematically compiled at county level. This hatched gap represents missing records, not zero production.</li>
                    <li><strong>Different Vintages from KNBS:</strong> HarvestStat and KNBS NAPR use different collection protocols and vintages. Absolute levels differ up to 2&times;; compare only within series.</li>
                  </ul>
                </div>
              </div>
              <div class="fold-footer-bar">

        <!-- Figure 4.4: Pastoral Terms of Trade (ToT) & Retail Market Prices -->
        <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-prices-card" style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;">
          <div class="enso-figure-header">
            <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
              <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
                <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 4.4</span>
                <h3 class="enso-figure-title">Pastoral Market Prices &amp; Terms of Trade (ToT) Monthly Purchasing Power — <span class="county-name-txt">Marsabit</span></h3>
              </div>
              <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Monthly retail food and livestock prices monitored across sentinel markets in <span class="county-name-txt">Marsabit</span> County (FEWS NET Data Warehouse). Evaluating purchasing power collapses during acute drought crises.</p>
            </div>
            <button class="provenance-link-btn" onclick="openMethodDrawer('market_prices')">Data &amp; Methodology</button>
          </div>

          <!-- ToT Ratio Formulation Callout -->
          <div style="background: #f0fdf4; border: 1px solid #bbf7d0; border-left: 4px solid #16a34a; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.85rem 1.15rem; margin-bottom: 1rem; font-size: 0.84rem; color: #166534; line-height: 1.5;">
            <strong>Terms of Trade (ToT) Economic Formulation &amp; Temporal Framing:</strong> Quantifies pastoral purchasing power as the kilograms of white maize grain purchased by selling one medium live goat:
            <div style="margin: 0.4rem 0; font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.95rem; font-weight: 700; color: #14532d;">
              ToT (kg maize / goat) = Retail Goat Price (KES / head) &divide; Retail Maize Grain Price (KES / kg)
            </div>
            In normal years across Marsabit, 1 goat purchases 60–75 kg of maize grain (2008–2020 climatological baseline median: 63.0 kg/goat). During severe droughts, grazing collapses force distress livestock dumping (depressing goat prices), while grain prices soar. When ToT falls below the <strong>25 kg/goat severe distress threshold</strong>, pastoral households experience catastrophic purchasing power collapse.<br>
            <strong>Methodological Framing Note:</strong> The severe &gt;50% purchasing power collapse holds strictly on <em>monthly purchasing power evaluated against trailing 24-month peaks</em> (August 2011: &minus;68.1% to 28.7 kg/goat; October 2022: &minus;65.4% to 33.4 kg/goat; February 2023: &minus;68.1% to 25.1 kg/goat across the full 2020&ndash;23 multi-season failure). Annual mean aggregation dampens these crisis troughs (2011: &minus;32.5%; 2022: &minus;37.6%) and masks acute seasonal distress. In addition, 2020 carries only 9 paired months in the sentinel series.
          </div>

          <!-- Controls Host for Figure 4.4 -->

            </div>
            <div style="position: absolute; top: 0; bottom: 0; left: 75%; width: 15%; background: rgba(43,131,186,0.18); border-left: 2px dashed #2b83ba;">

            </div>
            <div style="height: 100%; display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: space-around; font-size: 0.78rem; font-weight: 600;">
              <div style="color: #0284c7;">1. Rainfall Anomaly (CHIRPS v3) &rarr; 5 consecutive failed seasons in 2020–2022</div>
              <div style="color: #16a34a;">2. Pasture Biomass (MODIS NDVI) &rarr; 63% deficit in late 2022; rapid flush to 148% in Nov 2023</div>

          </div>
          <div style="font-size: 0.73rem; color: #64748b; margin-top: 0.35rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; line-height: 1.4;">
            &bull; <strong>IPC Licence Compliance (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO):</strong> Acute food insecurity phase classifications are published under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 IGO. Phases are displayed and cited directly as contextual benchmarks and linked out; they are not blended into CC-BY-4.0 derived analytical layers.
          </div>

          <!-- Folded Methods -->
          <details class="enso-more-details" style="margin-top: 1rem;">
            <summary>
              <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
              <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('market_prices')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
            </summary>
            <div class="methods-fold-content">
              <div class="decision-box">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                  <span class="rationale-tag">Causal Transmission Mechanism</span>
                </div>
                <p class="rationale-text">
                  <strong>The "Best Available Data" Reality:</strong> Meteorological drought does not directly starve people; the <em>market terms of trade</em> do. The FEWS NET Data Warehouse (USAID) provides monthly retail and wholesale price monitoring across sentinel markets in 42 counties (2000–2026). This connects oceanic temperature anomalies directly to pastoral household purchasing power and acute hunger.
                </p>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-grid">
                <div class="rationale-col">
                  <div class="rationale-heading">
                    <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                  </div>
                  <ul class="rationale-list">
                    <li><strong>Mandatory Detrending:</strong> Nominal Kenyan Shilling prices are deflated using national CPI and detrended to isolate climate shock spikes.</li>
                    <li><strong>Terms-of-Trade (ToT) Ratio &mdash; derived, not sourced:</strong> Quantifies the purchasing power of pastoralists as the kilograms of maize grain purchased by the sale of one medium live goat. We compute it here as goat price &divide; maize price from the FEWS NET series; no agency publishes it. Being a ratio, a fall can mean <em>either</em> cheaper livestock <em>or</em> dearer grain &mdash; opposite implications for a herder &mdash; so read it alongside the two price legs above, never alone.</li>
                  </ul>
                </div>
                <div class="rationale-col">
                  <div class="rationale-heading">
                    <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                  </div>
                  <ul class="rationale-list">
                    <li><strong>Sentinel Market Bias:</strong> Prices are recorded in primary subcounty hubs (Marsabit Town, Moyale, North Horr); remote nomadic camps face substantial unrecorded transport markups.</li>
                    <li><strong>Cross-Border Trade Flows:</strong> Unofficial livestock inflows from southern Ethiopia during regional crises can depress local livestock prices independently of Marsabit rainfall.</li>
                    <li><strong>Food Insecurity Benchmark &amp; Licence (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO):</strong> Official IPC acute food insecurity phases (Phases 1–5) and humanitarian caseload numbers are published by the IPC Global Support Unit and Kenya Food Security Steering Group (KFSSG). In accordance with CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO, IPC data are presented strictly for non-commercial reference and cited verbatim; they are never blended or merged into CC-BY-4.0 derived analytical layers.</li>
                  </ul>
                </div>
              </div>

                  <strong>The "Whole-of-System" Trade Reality:</strong> Drought does not respect administrative borders, but neither do regional food markets. The FEWS NET East Africa Cross-Border Trade (XBT) monitoring system tracks formal and informal commodity movements across 34 border crossing points throughout the Greater Horn of Africa (2010–2024). Measuring these trade flows reveals how regional spatial variability in rainfall buffers national food availability when Kenya experiences widespread Long or Short Rains failures.
```
